name: Solvang Duster
description:
A knee-length to ankle-length duster in heavy waxed cotton canvas, cut generously through the shoulders and chest with a back split that runs from hem to mid-thigh for ease of movement. Solvang makes this coat in three lengths and four weights; the most popular is the mid-weight in tobacco brown or charcoal, with antique brass press-studs down the front and at the wrist adjusters. The lining is a printed flannel in a small geometric pattern — different every season, always muted. The wax finish gives the coat a slight sheen that develops a patina over years of wear, acquiring creases and darker marks at stress points that become part of the garment's character.

Solvang is a Tier 3 Norwegian-heritage label that has been in the corridor since the 2140s. The duster occupies a comfortable space between working coat and considered fashion — it reads differently depending on who's wearing it and where. On a Tier 3 professional it says deliberate; on a Tier 2 worker it says inherited or saved up for; on a geneware user with a tail or modified lower body it says practical, because the generous cut and back split accommodate anatomy that most coats don't. People who move through multiple zones in a day — fixers, journalists, independent contractors — favor it for exactly that reason.
what_it_says: You move through the world on your own terms and you dress for that movement.
worn_by: anyone who covers ground between zones
story_hooks: A long-term owner's duster has had its wax finish re-applied so many times that the collar is nearly stiff — and pressed into the underside of the collar is the faint impression of a stamp, possibly a corponation seal, that wasn't put there by Solvang
Solvang's flannel lining pattern this season contains a repeated geometric element that a textile analyst claims is a compressed data glyph — the company has not responded to inquiries
Two people show up to the same meeting wearing the same coat in the same color, bought in the same season — one of them is not who they say they are

physical_description.visual_profile: A commanding knee-to-ankle duster with a deliberate, utilitarian silhouette that carries understated heritage. The coat drapes with authority—broad across the shoulders, tapering subtly at the waist, with a dramatic rear split that suggests both practicality and a hint of theatrical movement. The waxed canvas catches light with a soft, aged sheen that deepens toward the hem. Worn by someone with augmented lower body anatomy, it reads as intelligent accommodation; worn by a corpo on inherited savings, it reads as curated restraint.
physical_description.fit: Generously cut through shoulders and chest with room for layering or augmentation. Relaxed but intentional taper through the torso. Back split from hem to mid-thigh allows unrestricted leg movement and accommodates non-standard body modifications. Wrist adjusters with studs provide precision fit at cuffs. Silhouette suggests 2150s-2200s workwear lineage—functional, never cramped.
physical_description.primary_material: Heavy waxed cotton canvas (mid-weight standard). The wax finish is applied and maintained to develop patina; each coat becomes darker, more textured over years. Interior lined in printed flannel—tactile, muted, seasonal variations.
physical_description.texture: Exterior: smooth with slight nap, develops creasing and shadow marks at stress points (elbows, shoulders, hem folds). The wax sits cool to touch, almost buttery. Stress points darken naturally, creating a relief map of wear. Interior flannel is soft, slightly napped, with fine geometric print.
physical_description.color_scheme: Tobacco brown or charcoal primary (most popular). Antique brass hardware develops verdigris patina. Interior flannel in muted colorways—slate, sand, sage, never vibrant. Over time, the waxed exterior develops darker pooling at creases.
physical_description.closures: Antique brass press-studs down the front (8-10 studs, spaced for overlap). Wrist adjusters with matching studs. No collar closure—designed to wear open or partially buttoned.
distinctive_features: Full rear split from hem to mid-thigh—signature Solvang design, accommodates augmented legs and tails
Antique brass studs that oxidize and develop character over years
Printed flannel lining with rotating seasonal patterns, always muted geometric
Waxed finish develops darker stress-point patina that is part of the aesthetic
Generously cut shoulders and chest for layering or augmentation accommodation
Hem likely sits at calf to ankle depending on wearer's proportions
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3 professional grade with Tier 2 aspirational crossover. A Tier 1 corpo wearing one signals inherited taste or deliberate slumming. A Tier 5 salvager in one signals a prized find or long-term savings goal.
physical_description.cultural_context: Signals someone who moves between zones with intention. Fixers, journalists, independent contractors, medical workers, geneware users with non-standard bodies. Worn by Tier 3 professionals as 'deliberate choice.' Represents Norwegian-heritage craftsmanship and 80+ years of corridor reputation. Reads as practical intelligence rather than fashion statement—though it is both.
physical_description.condition_typical: Ranges from pristine (new purchase) to heavily patinated (5+ years wear). Most examples show visible stress-point darkening at shoulders, elbows, and hem folds. Wax finish may show slight cracking at deep creases—this is considered desirable aging. Flannel lining often more worn than exterior. Over time, the coat becomes more visually distinctive, never looking 'broken.'
